Respondent-Information Arms: Manuscript Comparisons

Luna and Muse across five prompt arms, replicating the manuscript’s comparison families

Published

September 14, 2026

Scope and method

The primary analysis covers Luna and Muse at N = 500, the two models carried furthest in this extension. A supplementary section repeats the same comparisons for a wider set of five models at N = 100, where every model has complete five-arm coverage but far fewer respondents.

Each cohort evaluates every model on the same first-N respondents of the frozen seed-42 sample, across five prompt arms:

Arm Information supplied
D demographic profile only
D+I profile plus the target-omitted ideal-point score
A only the other 29 observed answers, no demographics
D+A profile plus the other 29 answers
D+A+I profile, other answers, and the score

Comparison families follow the manuscript implementations in Code/Boris/: individual accuracy and PRE (compare plus party-pre.R), aggregate accuracy (calculate aggregate accuracy.R), regression weights (regression weights.R), rare profiles (rare profiles.R), and joint ideal-point fits (evaluate-pilot-local.R).

Two baselines recur. PRE is the proportional reduction in error against the pooled binary-majority rule. Party PRE is against each respondent’s own party’s majority on that question, estimated from the full 17,949-respondent human source rather than from the cohort.

Luna and Muse, N = 500

Individual accuracy

Proportional reduction in error

Proportional reduction in error against the pooled binary-majority rule: the share of the majority rule’s errors that the model avoids. Zero means no better than always predicting the more common answer.

Model D A only D+A D+I D+A+I
Luna 0.347 0.445 0.455 0.372 0.444
Muse 0.316 0.466 0.478 0.349 0.473

D+A performs best and D worst. Swapping demographics for the other answers improves it substantially. Of the gap to a perfect score left open by demographics alone, A only closes 19% and D+A closes 20%. On the measure’s own scale that is A only 37% better and D+A 41% better. Adding the ideal-point score moves it slightly on top of demographics alone and hardly at all on top of demographics-plus-answers.

Party PRE

The same reduction, but against each respondent’s own party’s majority on that question, estimated from the full 17,949-respondent human source. A negative value means the model does worse than simply applying the party stereotype.

Model D A only D+A D+I D+A+I
Luna 0.028 0.174 0.189 0.065 0.172
Muse -0.017 0.206 0.224 0.031 0.216

D+A performs best and D worst. Swapping demographics for the other answers improves it substantially. Of the gap to a perfect score left open by demographics alone, A only closes 19% and D+A closes 20%. Adding the ideal-point score moves it slightly on top of demographics alone and hardly at all on top of demographics-plus-answers.

Share of individual answers matching the respondent’s real answer. Reported for completeness; it rewards predicting the common answer and so is less informative than PRE.

Aggregate accuracy

Mean absolute error in support proportion

Aggregate accuracy: the mean absolute gap between the model’s and the survey’s support proportion, averaged over the 30 issues. This is a population-level measure, so individual errors in opposite directions cancel.

Model D A only D+A D+I D+A+I
Luna 0.1181 0.0991 0.0897 0.1219 0.0968
Muse 0.0830 0.0914 0.0783 0.0942 0.0825

D+A performs best and D+I worst. Swapping demographics for the other answers improves it slightly. Of the gap to a perfect score left open by demographics alone, A only closes 5% and D+A closes 16%. Adding the ideal-point score moves it moderately on top of demographics alone and slightly on top of demographics-plus-answers.

Majority direction correct (% of 30 issues)

Share of the 30 issues where the model gets the majority direction right, regardless of the size of the gap.

Model D A only D+A D+I D+A+I
Luna 86.7 86.7 90.0 86.7 80
Muse 86.7 76.7 83.3 83.3 80

D performs best and D+A+I worst. Swapping demographics for the other answers worsens it substantially. Of the gap to a perfect score left open by demographics alone, A only widens it 38% and D+A closes 0%. On the measure’s own scale that is A only 6% worse. Adding the ideal-point score moves it moderately on top of demographics alone and substantially on top of demographics-plus-answers.

Signed aggregate bias

Signed aggregate gap: positive means the model overstates support across issues, negative means it understates. Zero is unbiased in level, which is compatible with large offsetting errors.

Muse -0.0509 -0.0370 -0.0314 -0.0681 -0.0375

A only is closest to zero and D+I departs from it most. Swapping demographics for the other answers improves it moderately. Of the gap to a perfect score left open by demographics alone, A only closes 31% and D+A closes 25%. Adding the ideal-point score moves it moderately on top of demographics alone and moderately on top of demographics-plus-answers.

Ideal points

Ideal-point mean absolute error

Mean absolute error between each respondent’s simulated and real ideal point, from a joint human/LLM fit. This asks whether the model places a person correctly on the latent scale, not whether it gets individual items right.

Model D A only D+A D+I D+A+I
Luna 0.776 0.281 0.422 0.682 0.421
Muse 0.862 0.248 0.296 0.801 0.320

A only performs best and D worst. Swapping demographics for the other answers improves it substantially. Of the gap to a perfect score left open by demographics alone, A only closes 68% and D+A closes 56%. Adding the ideal-point score moves it slightly on top of demographics alone and hardly at all on top of demographics-plus-answers.

Correlation with the human ideal point

Correlation between simulated and real ideal points across respondents: whether the model gets the ordering of people right, ignoring scale and offset.

Model D A only D+A D+I D+A+I
Luna 0.719 0.943 0.905 0.824 0.918
Muse 0.715 0.966 0.955 0.867 0.956

A only performs best and D worst. Swapping demographics for the other answers improves it substantially. Of the gap to a perfect score left open by demographics alone, A only closes 84% and D+A closes 75%. On the measure’s own scale that is A only 33% better and D+A 30% better. Adding the ideal-point score moves it moderately on top of demographics alone and hardly at all on top of demographics-plus-answers.

Mean signed ideal-point error

Signed ideal-point error. Negative means the model places respondents further left than they are; positive, further right. Invisible to accuracy and PRE.

Model D A only D+A D+I D+A+I
Luna -0.402 -0.117 -0.160 -0.381 -0.167
Muse -0.017 -0.069 -0.065 -0.005 -0.046

A only is closest to zero and D departs from it most. Swapping demographics for the other answers improves it substantially. Of the gap to a perfect score left open by demographics alone, A only closes 56% and D+A closes 47%. Adding the ideal-point score moves it slightly on top of demographics alone and hardly at all on top of demographics-plus-answers.

Polarization ratio

Polarization ratio: the simulated Democrat-Republican median gap divided by the real one. Values above 1 mean the model exaggerates the partisan divide; 1.0 would reproduce it.

Model D A only D+A D+I D+A+I
Luna 2.77 1.3 1.74 2.66 1.72
Muse 4.56 1.3 1.49 4.26 1.52

A only comes closest to the reference value and D is furthest from it. Every arm overshoots it. Swapping demographics for the other answers improves it substantially. Of the gap to a perfect score left open by demographics alone, A only closes 89% and D+A closes 77%. Adding the ideal-point score moves it slightly on top of demographics alone and hardly at all on top of demographics-plus-answers.

Deviation densities

Distribution of each respondent’s simulated minus real ideal point, by arm. A curve centred away from the dashed line places people systematically to one side; a tall narrow curve means the model compresses distinct people toward a single position.

The same deviations split by the respondent’s real party, one row per arm. This is the mechanism behind the pooled signed bias: where the parties are displaced in opposite directions, a near-zero pooled figure conceals large errors in both.

Supplementary: broader model comparison

The section below repeats every comparison for a wider set of models, but on only 100 respondents. It is included for breadth across model families rather than precision: arm rankings there move materially with sample size, as the Luna and Muse series from N = 25 to N = 500 demonstrates. Treat the primary section above as the estimate and this one as context.

Deviation densities

Distribution of each respondent’s simulated minus real ideal point, by arm. A curve centred away from the dashed line places people systematically to one side; a tall narrow curve means the model compresses distinct people toward a single position.

The same deviations split by the respondent’s real party, one row per arm. This is the mechanism behind the pooled signed bias: where the parties are displaced in opposite directions, a near-zero pooled figure conceals large errors in both.

Limitations

  • The N = 100 cohort has 100 respondents per cell, so its rare-profile cells are small and its estimates are correspondingly noisy. The manuscript’s own rare-profile table uses min_n = 100 per cell, which no extension cohort can currently meet; the threshold here is 20 and every cell reports its count.
  • Black Republicans, the manuscript’s sharpest rare-profile case, do not reach the threshold in any cohort.
  • Ideal-point fits are single-chain at 10,000 iterations with fixed party starts. They are joint human/LLM fits, so scores are on a common scale within a fit but not across fits.
  • Aggregate accuracy is computed on the cohort, while party baselines come from the full human source. That follows the manuscript, but means aggregate and party-PRE numbers rest on different denominators.
  • These are exploratory paired comparisons, not significance tests.
